items.question: How can they come back?
items.text:
The books do speak to this, and the way back is the same road walked in reverse.

- **Repent and turn.** Jeremiah's whole message was "Turn away from your wicked ways. Stop doing evil! Repent and come back to God." That call still stands for anyone who has drifted [2].

- **Reason with God.** "Come now, and let us reason together" (Isaiah 1:18). God is a rational Being who wants to reason with you, so you do not have to put your mind aside to come back to Him — bring your honest questions to Him rather than letting them harden into doubt [3].

- **Pray.** Jesus told His disciples to pray because they might fall into temptation, and the strength to stand comes through prayer. A Christian who does not pray will fall into one temptation after another until he backslides, so prayer is where the return begins [7].

- **Commit yourself somewhere.** God expects the believer to be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, and every Christian must be planted in the house of the Lord. You need somebody to relate to as your pastor, because God made us like sheep who need a shepherd — you need to belong somewhere [7].

- **Adapt to your new circumstances.** The Israelites hung their harps on the willows in a strange land, but you can still sing the Lord's song wherever you are. If a new marriage, a new baby, a new job or a new city has cooled you, rise up and adapt rather than turning your back on God [5].

- **Stop looking back.** Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:17). If you keep remembering your past sinful life with nostalgia, you will turn into a pillar of salt; the way back is forward, not backward [8].

- **Do not presume on time.** There is a point of no return, and some who plan to backslide and return later forget that they may cross a line they cannot recross. Come back now, while it is called today [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 7 and 8 of *Backsliding* and chapter 3 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 19:17; Psalms 118:14; Psalms 137:4; Proverbs 7:10; Isaiah 1:18.

items.question: What is true forgiveness?
items.text:
True forgiveness is a releasing, not just a feeling. To forgive is to release all hurts, bitterness and wickedness from your heart in such a way that Satan stares in shock at a closed door to your heart — denying access to a horde of demons that are waiting [6].

Practically, that release takes shape in several ways: dismissing the thorny, painful issues; giving up all claims against the one who offended you; cancelling any indebtedness toward them; making no more mention of the matter; stopping resentment and anger; and cancelling any punishments you had planned for them [6]. It is to be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven you (Ephesians 4:32) [6].

Forgiveness also means leaving vengeance to God rather than taking it into your own hands. "Vengeance is mine, says the Lord" (Romans 12:19), so you submerge that feeling and trust Him to do the avenging [3]. Jesus Himself taught us to pray night and day for God to avenge us (Luke 18:6-8), and He taught that genuine forgiveness and the prayer for vengeance go together [3]. God has a repayment plan for all who harm you, and He will not be slack (Deuteronomy 7:9-10) [3].

And forgiveness is a choice you make, not something done to you — you are the key to your own recovery, and whether you get healed, or how soon, depends on you [1].

items.question: I keep saying hurtful things when I am angry. How do I control my mouth?
items.text:
It's a hard thing to watch your own words wound the people you love, and to feel you can't stop it. There is real help here.

- **See the tongue for what it is.** The tongue is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison, and no man can tame it on his own — it takes the Holy Spirit to help a believer control his tongue [3]. So begin by asking Him for help rather than trusting your own willpower.

- **Recognise that your words carry real power.** Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:21), and many words spoken are living spirits performing things in the physical realm [3][7]. What you say in anger is not harmless venting.

- **Deal with the anger underneath.** Wrath, anger, clamour and slander are all signs of lingering unforgiveness, and Scripture says to put them all away and be kind, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven you (Ephesians 4:31-32) [5]. Get the offence off your chest by walking in forgiveness, and don't let the sun go down on your wrath (Ephesians 4:26) [1].

- **Refuse to give the devil a foothold.** "Neither give place to the devil" (Ephesians 4:27) [1][6]. Angry outbursts open a door you don't want opened.

- **Let your words build instead of tear down.** Let no corrupt communication come out of your mouth, but only what is good for edifying, that it may minister grace to the hearers (Ephesians 4:29) [1].

- **Guard what you take in, too.** Watch out for the words you hear, because many of them are living spirits [7]. What fills you will eventually come out.

- **Keep your heart free of hurts.** A senior minister once advised, "Always keep your heart pure and free of hurts," and the years proved how important that advice was [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 60 of *Model Marriage*, chapter 1 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*, chapter 5 of *Why Few Are Chosen*, chapter 4 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*, chapter 2 of *Seven Great Principles* and chapter 13 of *Victory Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 18:21; 2 Corinthians 10:5; Galatians 5:13; Ephesians 4:26-27; Ephesians 4:29; Ephesians 4:31-32; James 3:8; Revelation 16:14.

items.question: What should I do when one of them is a leader I trained?
items.text:
That is a particular kind of pain — pouring yourself into someone and then watching them walk away. The books speak to it.

First, guard your own heart from bitterness. When a leader you trained leaves, the temptation is to speak evil of them or to "muddy the waters" you once drank from, and Scripture warns that this invites a curse into your life: "Whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house" (Proverbs 17:13) [1][2]. Instead, be grateful for the years you had together and speak well of where you came from, which gives you credibility [1].

Second, do not be surprised. Jesus knew the truth about Peter — that he would deny Him and go back to fishing — and He did not change the plans He had for him; in the end Peter became a great leader of the church, because truth mixed with grace can do that [8]. The same grace that restored Peter is available for the one who left you.

Third, examine yourself honestly. A departure can be permitted by God as judgment for a leader's sins, as when He allowed Baasha to rebel against Jeroboam's house [1]. Ask whether you left your people ignorant of loyalty, whether you stopped following the Lord as at first, or whether you failed to exert your authority [4][6].

Fourth, if they have already gone, let them go quickly. A little leaven leavens the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6), and one dissenting person pollutes the others with a disgruntled attitude [5]. Do not try to win back the hearts of your members by making special friends of them, for that leaves a confused congregation [1][2].

And if you must part ways, do it honourably — give ample notice, resign alone, and never set up next door to the church you left [1][2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 10 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapter 4 of *Ministerial Ethics*, chapter 5 of *Those who leave you*, chapter 4 of *Those Who Forget* and chapter 80 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 31:20-22; Numbers 16:3; Numbers 16:8-9; Proverbs 17:13; Ezekiel 34:18; John 13:27; John 13:38; John 21:2-3; 1 Corinthians 5:6.

items.question: Why do some Christians who give tithes prosper while others struggle?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
It's a question many faithful givers carry quietly, and the books speak to it directly.

The tithe is meant to be the first fruits of your increase, not the last fruits of your surplus — the first thing you do with your money, a ministration of respect and honour to God [7]. When it is not done first, it changes in its very nature, and that may be why someone gives ten percent and still sees no increase [7]. The tithe also simply means ten percent; nine percent is not a tithe, and God honours the full ten percent of your increase [7].

Beyond that, several things can neutralize the blessing a tither invokes:

- **Wrong desires.** If you have desires to kill and to fight, God cannot bless you; you may open the windows of Heaven only to have angels opposing you from another angle, for all things work together for your good [1].
- **Strife with the brethren.** The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by peaceful men, and faith works by love; strife is not something God will bless [1].
- **A troubled marriage.** Strife, bitterness and unforgiveness in a marriage can hinder your prayers, as 1 Peter 3:7 says, and so neutralize the blessing [1].
- **Hidden sin.** He that covers his sins shall not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy (Proverbs 28:13); hidden sin fights the blessing you invoke by tithing [1].
- **An unacceptable offering.** Money entering the offering bowl does not mean it was accepted in Heaven; offerings can be unacceptable because of an unrighteous life, secret idolatry, or not giving in proportion to what you received [7].

So the counsel is to examine the whole life, not just the amount given.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 22 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*.

Scriptures referenced: Nehemiah 12:43-44; Proverbs 28:13; James 3:18; James 4:2-3; 1 Peter 3:7.

items.text:

items.question: How can my wife and I build a strong marriage?
items.text:
Building a strong marriage is a good and worthy aim, and our books have much to say about how a home like that is built.

- **Make Christ the foundation and head of your home.** A home built on Him is like a house founded on rock, which the flood could not shake (Luke 6:47,48) [2]. When God is the focus of both of you, your closeness to Him draws you closer to each other; when He is the focus of only one, or of neither, the home grows stale or the couple drifts apart [2].

- **Apply biblical principles and build your marriage around the church.** The Word of God is your manual for marriage, and the one who delights in God's law is like a tree planted by rivers of water, bearing fruit in season (Psalm 1:1-6) [2]. Through wisdom a house is built and by understanding it is established (Proverbs 24:3) [2].

- **Develop family worship together.** Hold regular devotions, sometimes together with the children, attend church services and be involved in church activities, sitting together in church, and train your children to value Sundays [2].

- **Think as a Christian spouse, not as one.** Do nothing out of selfish ambition, but in humility consider others better than yourselves (Philippians 2:3) [2]. Reconcile the plans you each held before marriage to suit the home, be willing to give up certain interests for its sake, and do not always insist on your own way [2][5].

- **Speak the truth in love to each other.** Speaking truth in love makes us grow up in Christ (Ephesians 4:15), and it makes married people grow closer to each other [4]. Be the best of friends, sharing every success, disappointment, joy and pain, and choose to speak life, since death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:21) [4].

- **Guard your friendships and nurture trust.** Have mutual friends as much as possible, and discontinue friendships that do not sit well with your spouse, so that the marriage stays stable [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7, 9 and 60 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 32:17-20; Psalms 1:1-6; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 18:21; Proverbs 24:3; Luke 6:47-48; Ephesians 4:15; Philippians 2:3; 1 John 4:18.

items.question: There is a woman in our church who manipulates and controls people. How do I deal with her?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this — it's a heavy and lonely thing to face in a congregation you love.

The books speak to this directly. A woman who manipulates and controls others is what they call a Jezebel spirit, and the first thing to know is that she can be defeated if she is identified [7]. She often hides behind a spiritual disguise — she may be a prophetess, a teacher of the Word, someone highly respected in the church, so that using the name of God disarms you and makes you feel unable to fight against her [1][6]. She is also a mistress of seduction and persuasion: gentle, sweet, and convincing, so that people do not even realise they are being charmed into doing her wishes [3].

The critical point is that one person crying foul will not correct or control a Jezebel; it takes the collective rebuke of church leadership [3]. God's complaint against Thyatira was not that Jezebel existed but that they *allowed* her — "thou sufferest that woman Jezebel" (Revelation 2:20) [3][7]. So do not let her operate unchecked [2].

Practically, that means confronting her openly rather than keeping your dignity and self-respect intact by staying silent [8]. Pastors often avoid rebuking an out-of-order wife or influential woman because they want to keep good relations with everybody, but if a Jezebel goes uncorrected you may lose everything [7]. The books tell of an assistant pastor who served his senior pastor faithfully for twenty-five years; the pastor's wife slapped a church member, the congregation rose up, the senior pastor resigned, and the whole ministry collapsed — and the assistant's lament was that they had never confronted her [7]. Another man of God said his greatest mistake was not stepping in long before, and that it cost him his church and twenty-five years of work [8].

Insist on being led by the Holy Spirit and not by any man or woman [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 4, 10, 17 and 21 of *Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order* and chapter 15 of *Can’t You Do
Just a Little Bit More?*.

Scriptures referenced: Revelation 2:20.

items.question: What does Loyalty and Disloyalty say about the stages of disloyalty?
items.text:
Bishop Dag Heward-Mills teaches that disloyalty never happens overnight — it is a process, and most people are unaware they are becoming disloyal [1]. He outlines eight stages a person passes through on the way to becoming a rebel [1].

- **An independent spirit.** The person becomes autonomous within the group; the rules no longer control him, and he obeys only the instructions he thinks are important [1].
- **Offence.** Hurts and offences open the door to treachery — Jesus said many would be offended and then betray and hate one another (Matthew 24:10) [3].
- **Passivity.** The offended person withdraws, sits unconcerned and uninvolved; Absalom said nothing for two whole years after Amnon wronged his sister [3][6].
- **The critical stage.** He moves from silence to noticing and magnifying faults, as Miriam did when she spoke against Moses [5][6].
- **The political stage.** He draws others into his ideas, gathering a following with phrases like "many people are saying…" [5][7].
- **Deception.** Rebels are grossly deceived; if they were not, they would not do what they do [7].
- **Open rebellion.** The deceived insurrectionist fights openly against authority, as Lucifer, Absalom and Judas did [4].
- **Execution.** The end of all rebels is the same — God will divinely displace and replace them, for rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft (1 Samuel 15:23) [4].

He urges leaders to know these stages both to kill any such tendency in themselves and to detect it in those they work with [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 22:18; Leviticus 20:17; Numbers 12:1; 1 Samuel 15:23; 2 Samuel 12:28; 2 Samuel 13:22; 2 Samuel 13:28; 2 Samuel 15:3; 2 Samuel 15:11; 2 Samuel 16:1 and 10 more.

items.question: People are spreading lies about me in the church. How should I respond?
items.text:
That is a painful thing to carry, and I'm sorry you're facing it.

Our books speak to this. First, don't let the stories spread fear in you — slanderers trade in fear and panic, but God has not given us a spirit of fear, only power, love and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7) [1]. Your trust belongs to the Lord, as the psalmist said when he heard the slander of many: "But I trusted in thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my God" [1].

Second, keep meditating on God's word rather than on the rumours. When rulers sat together and slandered him, the psalmist said, "your servant will meditate on your decrees" [1].

Third, remember that God will deal with the slanderer in time; you do not have to avenge yourself [1].

Fourth, guard your own tongue in return. Slander is evil because it spreads a brother's failings instead of helping him rise again, and the Lord says, "Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm" (Psalm 105:15) [6]. Don't become what you're suffering from.

Fifth, if the lies are coming from someone in leadership, know that slander from a leader is especially devastating because their authority gives credence to the stories [1]. Take it to God and to wise counsel.

And sixth, be encouraged: those who mocked and conspired against God's servant in time faced trouble themselves, and some came back asking for prayer and forgiveness [2]. God sees, and He is not silent forever.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Those Who Are Slanderers* and chapter 7 of *One of You is a Devil*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; Psalms 31:11-14; Psalms 105:15; Psalms 119:21-24; Proverbs 11:13; 2 Timothy 1:7.

items.question: What does it mean to be a shepherd over a small group of people?
items.book: What It Means to Become a Shepherd
items.text:
Being a shepherd over a small group is a high honour, and it means caring for the people God has placed in your care.

- **You are a caring, loving guide.** A shepherd is simply someone God has called to look after sheep — people who need love, care and guidance [3]. Being a shepherd means you see people as sheep and relate to them as such [1].

- **You feed them.** Jesus told Peter to prove his love by feeding and caring for the sheep: "If you love me, feed my sheep" (John 21:16) [3][4]. The sheep are dependent on you for food, and it is a privilege to feed God's people [4].

- **You lead and guide them.** A shepherd leads his sheep beside still waters and to green pastures (Psalm 23:2), and guides them even through wilderness situations (Psalm 78:52-54) [5]. Leadership is an important privilege of shepherds [4].

- **You keep the family together.** A good shepherd keeps the church family together under his wings, holding old and young, married and unmarried, even enemies, in the same fold [7].

- **You notice their problems.** The good shepherd sees the wolf coming (John 10:12) — he knows when his people are doing exams, when they are having marital problems [7].

- **You share the burden.** The burden of praying, visiting, counselling and interacting with the sheep is not meant to be borne by one person alone; shepherds share it [8].

- **You are chosen and honoured.** It is a great honour to be chosen from among men and to have a job in things pertaining to God [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 5 and 13 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapters 2 and 3 of *The Privilege* and chapter 20 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:1-2; Psalms 77:20; Psalms 78:52-54; Psalms 95:6-7; Matthew 9:36; John 10:12; John 21:15-17.

items.question: How can I pray more effectively?
items.text:
Prayer that works is not about technique but about drawing near to God in the ways He has shown us. Here are some ways the books describe effective prayer.

- **Pray the Word.** Let your prayers be guided by Scripture, praying the very prayers recorded in the Bible — for instance Ephesians 1:17-19 and Ephesians 3:15-19, which ask God for wisdom, revelation, and to be grounded in love [1]. Become a Word person and believe the Word more than you believe in yourself [1].

- **Pray fervently.** Effective prayer is passionate, ardent, and eager — not doodling and dawdling [1]. If someone watched you pray, they should be able to describe it with words like burning or zealous [1].

- **Pray in tongues.** Spend hours praying in tongues, using the gift God has given; Paul said, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [1].

- **Talk with the Holy Spirit.** Prayer is a two-way affair — speak to Him and hear Him speak back, for He is to us what Jesus was to His disciples [1]. Those who hold conversations with the Holy Spirit are often very advanced in their walk with God [1].

- **Pray long.** Jesus rose a great while before day and prayed, and continued all night in prayer to God (Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12) [1]. His example is compelling enough to follow [1].

- **Pray at set times and without ceasing.** Develop the habit of praying morning, afternoon, evening, and all-the-time, for "pray without ceasing" (1 Thessalonians 5:17) [3][5]. Morning prayer meets God before you meet the devil [5].

- **Watch and pray.** Staying awake at night to pray lets you pray far more hours than those who only fast and pray [7].

items.question: How can a young person stay away from sexual sin?
items.text:
You're asking a question the books take seriously, and they answer it with real hope for young people.

- **Respect your desires instead of denying them.** Your sexuality is something to be respected, and a proper respect for youthful lusts, rather than a denial of them, will save you from them [4]. Young people sense strong sexual urges that constantly remind them of their lack of holiness, and that feeling removes their confidence in the things of God [5].

- **Know that God's will for you is purity.** As 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4 says, the will of God is your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality [3]. Since that is one of the clearest directions of the Lord, make it one of your clearest and most energetic goals to practically live a sexually pure life [3].

- **Find your own way of staying free.** Everyone has a different way by which he keeps himself from fornication, and you must find out what God's will is for your own journey of staying away from it [3]. It may be God's will for you to avoid certain books or films, certain friends, or certain places [3].

- **Avoid untimely relationships.** Very young people should not enter into courtship relationships, for as Ecclesiastes 3:1 says, there is a season and a time to every purpose under heaven [6]. Enter only into relationships that lead to marriage, since the only intimate relationship between men and women that God approves of is marriage [6].

- **Turn away from riotous living.** Fooling around with the opposite sex is riotous living, and that is exactly what destroyed the young man in the story of the prodigal son [7]. If you develop a taste for a different girl every other day, it becomes difficult to live happily ever after with one woman [7].

- **Be visible, not hidden.** Sit in the front in church and in class, and make sure your pastor knows your name, because people who sit far away are often practicing some kind of evil and do not want to be noticed [7].

- **Know that holiness is possible for you.** Holiness is engineered by the Spirit of holiness, not by being an older person; age has nothing to do with holiness [8]. Every young person can be empowered by the Spirit of holiness to become whatever God wants him to become [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapters 10, 13 and 24 of *Ready@20*, chapter 35 of *The Art of Shepherding* and chapter 4 of *Spiritual Dangers*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:16; Psalms 119:9; Ecclesiastes 3:1; Jeremiah 2:5; Matthew 19:16-20; Luke 15:13; Luke 15:15; Luke 15:30; John 8:46; Romans 1:4 and 5 more.

items.question: How can I tell when someone in my team is becoming disloyal?
items.text:
Disloyalty rarely announces itself; it grows quietly, and the books give you several things to watch for.

- **An independent spirit.** The first stage is subtle: a person still belongs to the group but becomes autonomous within it, no longer controlled by its rules, obeying only the instructions he thinks are important and attending only the meetings he judges worthwhile [1].

- **Absence in times of pressure.** Watch how people behave when the church is under strain, for it is in the heat of events that true character shows; some simply absent themselves when things are hard [2].

- **Inflexibility and resistance to correction.** An inflexible person is stubborn and defiant, unwilling to go beyond what is stipulated, unwilling to adapt, and unwilling to take correction when confronted — Saul argued with Samuel even when the evidence of his disobedience was plain [3].

- **Silence and quiet satisfaction when things go wrong.** An assistant who has no comment, good or bad, on your suggestions may not be in full agreement, and one who is glad when something fails was never in full support of it [4].

- **Criticism, murmuring and fault-finding.** Where members constantly criticise their leader, undermine their pastors, accuse and find fault, there is demonic activity at work, and leaders often mistake it for a bad attitude [7].

- **A concern for his own image above yours.** A dissatisfied assistant resents the differences that make him subordinate and wants the same authority, status and possessions as his head [4].

And remember, loyalty today does not guarantee loyalty tomorrow — one brother proclaimed his commitment loudly for years, then quietly pulled out and took church property with him [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 5 and 8 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapters 4 and 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 5 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 1:5-7; John 2:24-25; John 6:70; John 7:3; John 7:5.

items.question: How should a Christian live simply and avoid wasting money?
items.text:
Wanting to live simply and stop wasting money is a good and godly desire, and our books have much to say about it.

- **Cut out waste deliberately.** Most poor nations waste half of their resources, which is exactly why they stay poor; the same is true of a person, so you must learn to prevent wastage in your own life [6]. When you can stop the things that waste away your money, you will become rich [1].

- **Avoid an expensive lifestyle.** Cut your coat according to your size, and do not follow others into grandiose and expensive things; do not be deceived by those who live large on money they actually owe [6]. Wasters are often deceived about how wealth is created, and so they destroy wealth by their lifestyles [1].

- **Choose your friends carefully.** The prodigal son did not waste his money alone — there were harlots helping him do it, and bad company will always be there to help you do bad things [3]. As 1 Corinthians 15:33 says, evil company corrupts good habits, so a born-again Christian should make friends with Christians [3].

- **Refuse get-rich-quick schemes.** Wise businessmen are wary of any "get-rich-quick" scheme, and one such bank collapsed and many people lost their money [4]. The Kingdom of Heaven is like a mustard seed that needs time to grow, so there are no short cuts in Christianity [4].

- **Deal with lust before it grows.** If you have any strange lusts in you, kill them now, or they will grow up and take over your life [5]. Lust for anything apart from God's Word is dangerous, because you will sacrifice so many things to get what you want [5].

- **Learn to do things with your own hands.** Do not sit aloof in an armchair imagining you are an executive; roll up your sleeves and work, and develop a dislike for loans and gifts [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapters 3 and 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 2 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 30:3-6; Psalms 27:4; Mark 4:19; Luke 15:12-14; Luke 15:25; Luke 16:1-2; 1 Corinthians 15:33.

items.question: What is the secret to answered prayer?
items.text:
What a good question to bring — the books speak to this often, and warmly.

- **Learn to pray for yourself.** God wants you to be able to come to your heavenly Father directly, not to depend only on your pastor or on prayer warriors; their prayers are a bonus, not your foundation [5].
- **Let God's Word abide in you.** God does not act outside His Word, and His Word directs you in prayer; He does not answer foolish prayers or anything against His Word, so stay in the Word [1][2].
- **Obey His commandments.** Scripture is clear that God answers the prayers of those who obey Him — as 1 John 3:22 says, we receive because we keep His commandments — and disobedience closes that door [1][2].
- **Be a fruit-bearing Christian.** God has linked answered prayer to bearing fruit; as John 15:16 says, we are chosen and ordained to bring forth fruit that remains, and He answers the one who bears fruit [2].
- **Stay in fellowship.** If you walk in the light you will have fellowship with others in the light, as 1 John 1:7 says; staying in fellowship is a key to receiving the Lord's blessings [2].
- **Persist, and also pray in faith.** Jesus taught both: praying over and over with determination until you get an answer, and praying once in faith — each is a valid expression of faith, and each brings results [3][8].

Both keys are failure-proof, so decide today to use them [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 4 of *100% Answered Prayer* and chapter 9 of *How to Pray*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 91:15; Psalms 119:133; Isaiah 58:9; Luke 11:5-9; John 15:16; 2 Corinthians 5:21; James 5:16; 1 John 1:7; 1 John 3:22.

items.question: In the book Backsliding, what are the signs that someone is falling away?
items.text:
The book names several symptoms that show a heart may be drifting from God. Here are the clearest ones.

- **Bad company.** A Christian who keeps bad friends is on a dangerous path, because bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33) and will eventually lead you to bad places [1]. The friends you move with will either lead you to church or away from it [1].

- **Stubbornness.** A person who will not heed counsel but always does what he wants, in spite of all advice, is a potential backslider [3]. The backslider in heart is filled with his own ways (Proverbs 14:14), and Scripture says there is safety in the multitude of counsel [3].

- **Praying less.** Prayer keeps us from falling, for Jesus said to pray lest you fall into temptation [4]. Anyone you spend time talking to becomes close to you, so a Christian who spends less time praying is unknowingly moving away from God [4].

- **Not being committed.** Anyone who does not want to be committed to a church will ultimately leave it [4]. God expects the believer to be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, and an uncommitted Christian is a potential backslider [4].

- **Coldness and murmuring.** Backsliding Christians first become aloof, diplomatic and uninterested, yawning and glancing at their watches during service [5]. Murmuring — complaining, grumbling and criticizing — is another sign; those who murmur and complain often leave their churches and eventually backslide [8].

- **Shallowness.** Some receive the Word with joy but have no root, and in the time of testing they fall away (Luke 8:13) [6]. A shallow Christian will fall at the next shaking or crisis [6].

- **Foolish questioning and curiosity.** Foolish and unlearned questions are to be avoided, for they gender strifes (2 Timothy 2:23) [5]. Curiosity, like the prodigal son's, has killed many a backslider [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5 and 7 of *Backsliding*.

items.question: A member has stopped coming to church and stopped praying. How do I help them come back to God?
items.text:
It's painful to watch someone you love drift, and it's right to want them home. Our books speak to this.

**Pray for them and travail for Christ to be formed in them.** Prayer is not a side activity here — without it you are wasting your time, and you should travail in birth for Christ to be formed in them, as Galatians 4:19 says [6]. Pray specifically that when they go, they will come back, and come back with more people [1][2].

**Understand what has happened to them.** Praying less is itself a symptom of backsliding: anyone you spend time talking to becomes close to you, so a Christian who stops praying is unknowingly moving away from God [8]. Not being committed follows the same path — anyone who does not want to be committed to a church will ultimately leave it, and an uncommitted Christian is a potential backslider [8].

**Go to them.** Visit new converts and visitors; physically going to homes is a powerful first step, and this is work many church members can be trained to share [6]. Encourage them, show them you really love them, and pray with them for the establishment of their soul [6].

**Call them back into fellowship.** Staying in fellowship is a key to receiving the Lord's blessings, and if you are walking in the light you will have fellowship with others who are in the light, as 1 John 1:7 says [3].

**Keep sowing, and don't be discouraged.** Whatever a man sows he will reap, as Galatians 6:7 says; after an outreach the results often come later, and God divinely sends people from that very place [5][7]. Do not be discouraged by fluctuating attendance — that is how sheep behave [5][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 11 and 20 of *Church Planting*, chapter 6 of *Ministerial Barrenness*, chapter 9 of *How to Pray*, chapters 7 and 10 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 7 of *Backsliding*.

items.question: How do I start a new church in a town where we have no members?
items.text:
It's a good and honest question, and our books have a great deal to say about it.

- **Count the cost first.** Sit down and consider what starting a church will really involve, because it will not be easy — as Luke 14:28 says, the one who builds a tower first counts the cost [1][2]. Expect to be despised and opposed in the early days, as many pioneers have been [1][2].

- **Do not become financially desperate.** Find a job and start the church as a lay person rather than depending on the new church for your survival; a small congregation cannot carry your salary, and desperation will show [1][2]. Money is needed for equipment and rent, and siphoning out the lifeblood of the church keeps it from developing normally [1][2].

- **Two or three is enough.** You do not need a crowd to begin — as Matthew 18:20 says, where two or three are gathered in His name, He is there among them [1][2]. One pastor who knew nobody in South Africa started a church there, and the work in Zürich began with one person known [1][2].

- **Don't be in a hurry.** No tree grows from a seed overnight, and a hasty spirit will not succeed; Proverbs 28:22 warns that he who hastens to be rich has an evil eye [8]. The kingdom is like a mustard seed — the least of seeds, which becomes the greatest among herbs [8].

- **Pray for and recruit pillars.** Ask God for labourers and helpers, then go out and recruit them, as Jesus called Simon, Andrew, James and John [8]. Be careful never to break down someone else's church to build your own, for you will reap what you sow (Galatians 6:7) [8].

- **Do not be discouraged by small or shifting numbers.** Fluctuating attendance and members rotating week by week is simply how sheep behave — take no notice of them [3][4]. One pastor preached to a single person in deep depression, and today that church is a megachurch [8].

- **You don't need the extras.** A complimentary card, briefcase, constitution, logo or flag are not vital at the start; what matters is members and a regular congregation [3][4]. Pray for them, preach the Word, visit the sheep and trust God — since the Greater One is in you, you cannot fail [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 28:22; Matthew 13:31-32; Matthew 18:20; Mark 1:16-17; Mark 1:19-20; Luke 14:28; Galatians 2:9; Galatians 6:7.

items.question: How do I deal with disloyal people?
items.text:
Dealing with disloyalty is one of the hardest things a leader faces, and the books speak to it plainly. Here are the ways they set out.

- **Teach your people constantly.** The teaching method is a preventive process: regularly teaching the Word immunizes people against deception, since it is only deceived people who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [4]. It is better to manage by prevention than to move from one crisis to another [4].

- **Dismiss them outright.** When Satan rebelled, he was sacked and cast out — not prayed for, not counselled, not rehabilitated [1]. God dealt with rebellion by casting it down, so you must do the same [1].

- **Cast out the scorner.** The biblical remedy for scoffers is not fasting or praying but casting them out — dismissing, expelling, ejecting, firing, laying off [6]. As Proverbs 22:10 says, cast out the scorner and contention, strife and reproach will cease [6][7].

- **Wipe out their associates too.** No friendship with a disloyal person is neutral; those who even "understand" them should not be part of your team [3]. God wiped out Lucifer and the angels associated with him, and you must do the same [3].

- **Restrict and bind them.** God used four principles on the devil: binding him, putting him in a bottomless pit, shutting him up and sealing him [8]. Allowing a disloyal person to operate freely after you know what he is makes you wiser than God [8].

- **Be fierce and resolute.** Treachery and treason have the power to end a ministry, so do not deal with the enemy in a spirit of benevolence [5]. One pastor's disloyal associate spread bad stories and left with almost the whole church, reducing three thousand members to about twenty [8].

items.question: What does the book Frugality say about spending on church buildings?
items.text:
The book doesn't treat church buildings as a special category of spending — it treats them as one more thing God has placed in your charge, to be handled with the same carefulness as everything else. So the counsel runs like this.

**Value the project by the Word, not by your own sense of what matters.** The Bible is what tells us what is important and good, and we are to obey it whether it sounds good or difficult [2]. A building is weighed by that standard, not by our feelings about it.

**Gather the crumbs on it.** Jesus fed five thousand, then told His disciples, "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost" (John 6:12), and they collected twelve baskets [4]. Bishop Dag Heward-Mills tells of the Lighthouse Cathedral project, where the Lord told him, "If you count your pennies, you will go very far" — and the church, with no big tycoon sponsoring it, gathered the crumbs and completed a multi-million cedi cathedral [4].

**Watch the waste that eats the funds.** He notes that in his church electricity, water and telephone bills are monitored on a chart, and staff share the phone bill when it goes above a set figure, because all of that contributes to the eventual wealth of the church [4].

**Store in the fat years for the lean ones.** Joseph told Pharaoh to store food during the years of plenty so Egypt would survive the lean years (Genesis 41:1-4), and the lean cows always eat the fat ones [8].

**Don't chase fantasies instead of the ground before you.** Proverbs 28:19 says the one who works his land will have abundant food, but the one who chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5, 6, 8 and 9 of *Frugality*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 41:1-4; Proverbs 22:1; Proverbs 28:19; Jeremiah 42:6; Micah 6:8; Matthew 12:39; Matthew 16:26; John 6:12; 1 Timothy 1:12.

items.question: What mistakes do pastors usually make that hurt their ministry?
items.book: The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make
items.text:
Here are the mistakes the books name most often, and how each one wounds a ministry.

- **Choosing to bear little fruit.** Some pastors leave fruitful ground for a place they simply want to live, and end up with forty members where they might have had a thousand; the desire for an address or a green card replaces the desire for fruit [1]. Others won't bear much fruit under someone else's banner, because independence matters more to them than fruitfulness [1].

- **Turning into a Pharisee.** After years in ministry it becomes easy to care about the best seats and who sits where; one pastor was publicly moved from the front row to the second, and another shunned a whole programme over seating [2].

- **Getting priorities wrong.** Building your own church is a greater priority than a nice car, and pastors who neglected it ended up poor and homeless; giving first place to the rich and powerful while setting aside the young and the poor lets a church die of stiffness and tradition [4].

- **Losing humility and childlikeness.** Pastors become the opposite of children, unable to be taught, never responding to an altar call, unwilling to look foolish — and so they cannot enter higher dimensions of the Kingdom, as Matthew 18:3 says [8]. Remaining small in your own eyes, teachable and a learner, is some of the best advice a pastor can receive [3].

- **No longer seeing yourself as a sheep.** Once ordained, many stop considering themselves as sheep, yet pastors still need to be led and guided and to pray constantly for direction [3].

- **Being slow about ministry.** Slowness in obeying God's call is dangerous, because the speed at which we move helps determine our lives [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 3, 7, 8 and 9 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make* and chapter 31 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:16-17; Matthew 18:3; Matthew 23:6-7; John 7:6; John 15:8.

items.question: What should I read during it?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
Our books give several ways to choose what you read.

- **Read through a book of the Bible a few verses at a time.** Pick a book and read a few verses each day, always remembering where you stopped so you can continue from that same place the next day [3][4][5]. The author names Luke and Ephesians in the New Testament, and Genesis and 1st and 2nd Samuel in the Old, as books he has had wonderful quiet times in [5].

- **Follow one Bible personality.** Choose a person from the Bible whose life story you follow, because a few verses from passages about Moses, for example, will give you much revelation for your life [3][4][8].

- **Use a daily reading guide.** Take the passage suggested in your daily reading guide; when he first became a Christian, the author depended on *Our Daily Bread* for his quiet time [3][4][8].

- **Let the Holy Spirit stop you.** Read slowly, don't take a very long passage unless it's necessary, and stop at any verse that strikes you — God's Word is so powerful that a single word in a verse is enough to change your life [3][8].

- **Go deeper where something strikes you.** When God ministers to you about something, be prepared to study further with a good reference Bible, looking for what the passage teaches about God, a promise to claim, a command to obey, a warning to heed, or a prayer to pray [3][4][8].

- **Keep the Word in you day and night.** Meditate on the word of God all the time, as Joshua 1:8 says, because that is what will soon be coming out of your mouth [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers*, chapter 3 of *The Secret*, chapter 10 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapter 11 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*.

items.question: Is it acceptable to use ChatGPT to write my sermons?
items.text:
I want to be honest with you rather than clever here, because this touches the heart of your calling.

The books speak a great deal about how a sermon must come from you. A pastor's greatest asset is his ability to preach and teach, and the best preachers are "heart preachers" and not "note preachers" — if the thing is not in your heart, don't bother to say it, because people notice when what you are saying does not come from your heart [5]. The powerful sermons in Acts were unrehearsed and from the heart; Peter stood and addressed the crowd without notes, and preparation is something that takes a long time to go deep down into your heart [5]. Preaching should also be Holy Spirit inspired and anointed, trusting the Spirit even when it runs contrary to your wonderfully prepared notes, for it is "not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, saith the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6) [5][3].

The books also insist that your preaching carry windows — illustrations, stories and personal life testimonies that let people see into your sermon and into your life; a pastor who will not open up about himself will never be a good preacher, and Jesus preached with windows all the time [3]. And the word you preach is a sharp, living sword that pulls down strongholds as you preach it [6].

So the question the books press on you is not really about the tool, but about whether the message is in your heart, anointed by the Spirit, and shaped by your own walk with God and knowledge of your people.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 4 of *Am I Good For Nothing?*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 130:1; Ezekiel 2:2; Zechariah 4:6; John 6:63; Acts 10:44; 1 Corinthians 9:22; 1 Corinthians 14:40; 2 Corinthians 10:4-5; 2 Timothy 4:2; Hebrews 4:12.

items.question: A teenager in our youth group says he cuts himself when he is sad.
items.text:
That is a heavy thing for a young person to carry, and I'm glad he told you.

The books speak directly to this. Self-harm is described as a manifestation of the presence of Satan — the madman of Gadara, under demonic influence, "cut himself with stones," systematically destroying himself [8]. Demons help people to destroy themselves [8]. So this is not merely a bad habit; it is a spiritual matter to be tackled at its root [3].

Depression is a powerful spirit that can lead people toward suicide, and it often shows itself in withdrawal — depressed people isolate themselves because they feel worthless, ashamed, and hopeless [6]. Elijah, who had called down fire from heaven, retreated into the wilderness when Jezebel threatened him and asked God to take his life [6]. So sadness this deep is not a sign that he is weak or far from God.

The counsel is to receive deliverance in the name of Jesus, for it was demons that made the madman cry out [3]. And bitterness and hurts kept inside are self-destructive — many destroy themselves by holding on to pain [8]. Help him bring what he is carrying into the light rather than bearing it alone.

If he is in danger of ending his life, please do not carry this by yourself; bring in those who can watch over him.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 9 and 11 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them* and chapter 22 of *Those who are mad*.

items.question: A leader I trained for years has just left the church. How do I handle it?
items.text:
This is a deep wound, and I'm sorry you're carrying it. Let me walk with you through what our books say.

First, examine your own heart before the Lord. Ask whether you have strayed from following Him as you did at the beginning, whether you have failed to exert your authority, or whether your leadership style contributed to this departure — while accepting that sometimes people stir up strife no matter how well you lead [5][4]. Be careful not to mock or despise anyone in trouble, for "he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished" (Proverbs 17:5) [3].

Then cleanse yourself of the evil seeds. A departure pollutes your spirit with hurt, anger, hatred, and revenge, and you will need to pray long and hard to get free, lest you fall into bitterness and unforgiveness [4].

Handle the leaver with God's wisdom, not your own. Binding a "Judas" means restricting him; allowing a disloyal person to operate freely is a great mistake of leaders who think they are walking in love [2]. And remove disloyal people quickly — if someone indicates a desire to leave, it is best they go immediately, for "a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6) [7].

Teach your people the Word on loyalty and disloyalty, for as you do, confusion will evaporate, since God is not the author of confusion (1 Corinthians 14:33) [4].

Finally, open your heart to what God is doing. Sometimes a departure heralds the arrival of God's choice for you — as when Saul's heart departed and David was revealed [6]. Let this become a stepping stone to a higher dimension of ministry [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets*, chapters 1 and 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 3 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

items.question: How do I deal with demonic attacks on my family?
items.book: Demons and How to Deal with Them
items.text:
I'm sorry your family is under this weight — that is a heavy thing to carry, and you are right to take it seriously.

The first thing the books would have you do is identify what you are actually facing, because naming the problem is most of the battle. Jesus asked the madman of Gadara, "What is thy name?" (Luke 8:30), and once the spirit was named it could be cast out; ask God to reveal the real identity of what is harassing your household [4]. Look for the marks: unusual, illogical behaviour that makes no sense points to demonic activity, as with the Gadarene who lived among the tombs and cut himself with stones (Mark 5:3, 5) [5]. So does persistence — trouble that keeps coming, one thing after another, as with Job, whose losses were Satan's direct attack (Job 1:12) [5]. And so does fear, which is the commonest sign of a demonic presence and has power to change the whole course of a life [8].

Then deal with it directly. Stealing, killing and destroying are the devil's work — Jesus said the thief comes to steal, kill and destroy, but He came to give life (John 10:10) — so bind those powers and destroy their plans rather than letting destroyers prosper around you [1]. Watch for strife too: quarrels and conflicts are demonic in nature (James 3:14-15), and the devil is ready to gather you into a battle if you yield, so refuse the fight [2]. Be sober and vigilant, because your adversary walks about seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8) [3]. And tighten your security: lies and deception of any kind expose you to invasion, so stay in the truth, as Ephesians 6:14 says, and practise righteousness rather than sin [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 8 and 18 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 14 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*, chapters 4 and 20 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them* and chapters 5 and 24 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

items.question: How do I forgive someone who hurt me very badly?
items.text:
I'm sorry you've been hurt so badly — that kind of pain is real, and it's not a small thing to carry.

The books give a clear picture of what forgiveness actually is, and how to get there. To forgive is to release all the hurt, bitterness and wickedness from your heart, so that you deny the enemy access to it [1]. Concretely, that means dismissing the thorny, painful issues, giving up your claims against the person, cancelling what they owe you, making no more mention of the matter, and cancelling any punishment you had planned for them [1][3].

One step that makes this easier is to analyse the offender. Jesus, as He was being killed, said, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34) — He made excuses for His own murderers [2]. Bishop Dag Heward-Mills tells of a junior pastor who once shouted and threatened him in front of a senior associate: instead of dismissing him, he said to himself, "He does not know what he is doing," and that made forgiveness possible [2]. Perhaps your offender is sick, ignorant or confused [2].

It also helps to analyse your own past sins, considering yourself lest you also be tempted [2]. Remember that you are equally in need of forgiveness from God — if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you (Matthew 6:14) [3].

And walk in love: pray for the one who hurt you, as Jesus prayed for those who persecuted Him [1][3]. Forgiveness is not the end of the story — you give place to God's wrath, for "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Romans 12:19) [6]. Your duty is to forgive; God's duty is to repay [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *Those Who Are Offended* and chapters 5 and 8 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*.

items.question: What does The Mega Church say about why churches need many pastors?
items.text:
Yes — the books speak to this directly. Here is what they say about why a church needs many pastors and ministers.

- **A large church releases more labourers into the harvest.** Jesus said the harvest is great but the workers are few, and told us to pray the Lord of the harvest to send out more workers (Matthew 9:37-38), so the larger the crowd, the more labourers are sent forth and the more easily they can be financed [2].

- **A large church produces more full-time ministers.** In a large church there is always a training programme that produces ministers, so a ten thousand member congregation will produce more pastors than a hundred member church; indeed, the pastor of a smaller church is not likely to have enough people who want to be ministers of the gospel [2].

- **More people means more prayer against the enemy.** In a mega church more people are involved in prayer against the power of the prince of the air, standing against principalities and powers with the whole armour of God [2].

- **Growth is God's will, and smallness is not the goal.** God's will is that His house may be filled, and Satan wants your church to remain small, for the fewer people you have the more captives he has [3].

- **A large church can meet many different needs.** A congregation is a group of people with varied needs, and in a large church you are likely to find a lawyer, a doctor, an engineer, a pharmacist or even a psychiatrist to serve them [7].

- **A large church can support special ministries.** As the church grows it becomes more diverse, and specialist ministries develop — to the poor, refugees and orphans — which a small church usually cannot sustain [1][4].

- **A large church becomes a force to reckon with.** As it increases in size it becomes a powerful community, almost a nation within a nation, and governments begin to fear its power and influence, while they despise small churches [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *The Mega Church*.

items.question: According to Church Growth, why do some churches stop growing?
items.text:
Some churches stop growing because they fail to share the burden of ministry. When the work rests on one person, the church can grow to a point and then come to a standstill — the burden of the ministry simply cannot be borne by one person [3]. Others hold back from sharing because they want all the glory for themselves, or because they fear an associate will rebel or outshine them, but you cannot expand without trusting people [3].

Another reason is the absence of a burning vision. A shallow or superficial vision for a large church will not make it grow; without a burning vision you will not spend the time seeking the wisdom that brings growth, you will grow irritated with the strategies taught, and you will criticize the very thing you need most [2][8]. It is the burning vision that gives the staying power and persistence for the long journey [8].

Isolation also holds a church back. Churches that do not grow are often isolated, and silently living in isolation will not help anybody who wants his church to grow [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 4 and 21 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 27:17; Proverbs 29:18; Ephesians 4:15-16.

items.question: And how should I deal with them once I notice it?
items.text:
Once you see it, the books are clear that you must act rather than tolerate it.

- **Teach constantly as prevention.** The first method is teaching the Word of God regularly, because teaching fights deception — it was deception that led Lucifer and Absalom astray, and the devil is called "that old serpent who deceives the whole world" [5]. Preventive management spares you the stress of moving from one crisis to another [5].

- **Cast the scorner out.** Proverbs 22:10 says, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea, strife and reproach shall cease" [6][8]. To cast out means to dismiss, expel, eject, banish, fire, sack, discard, unseat or lay off [8]. Failure to dismiss someone who must go is weak leadership — it is like allowing a snake to live under your children's bed [8].

- **Wipe out their associates too.** Friendship with a disloyal person is never neutral; God cast out Lucifer and the angels associated with him, and you must release those who are friends of your traitors to join the enemy camp openly [1].

- **Dismiss questionable loyalties.** A leader must refuse to lead people who are mysterious, secretive and questionable in their loyalty, since failing to remove them lets a root of bitterness grow until many are defiled [6]. Absolute evidence is not even needed — being a mysterious person is deemed enough [7].

- **Provide for longstanding workers.** Even if someone has served fifty years, dismissal is still essential, but in keeping with mercy and compassion, make financial provision so they can live and work elsewhere without undue hardship [7]. This prevents the root of bitterness from spreading, as Hebrews 12:15 warns [7].

- **Mark and avoid.** Romans 16:17, 18 teaches that those who cause divisions must be noted and avoided; to mark means to brand or label so the person stands out and can be recognized from afar [8].

- **Sometimes simply release them peacefully.** This differs from throwing out a rebel: when someone told Bishop Dag he did not believe in his prayer, he told the man to go peacefully to another church, and with time the differences showed, as they did after Abraham and Lot separated [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Now We Are At War*, chapter 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 77 of *The Gift Of Governments*.

items.question: What does 'The Art of Shepherding' teach about visiting members?
items.text:
The books speak to this, and they treat visiting as part of the shepherd's plain duty.

A shepherd is to function by praying for the sheep, visiting them, counselling them and interacting with them [5]. That is set alongside David's own habit of rising early and leaving the sheep with a keeper while he went where he was sent [5].

Visiting is especially for times of trouble. A shepherd must be there when the trouble is at its peak — found standing by the grave, in the hospital, at the operating theatre, by the bedside, or wherever the trouble has struck [6]. The contrast is drawn sharply: bad shepherds visit the sheep to get money from them when they are rich, but good shepherds are there in times of trouble [6].

There is also a warning about the opposite kind of shepherd. Jesus said that the hireling, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf catches them and scatters them (John 10:12) [6]. A hireling does not even see when the sheep are dying, while a good shepherd notices when his sheep are in distress, even in little things [6].

And visiting belongs with feeding. If you do not have the time or heart to gather the people you lead and gently carry them along, you will never have the chance to feed them; without that gentleness the sheep will not be open to receive from the shepherd [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 23, 27 and 32 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 16:23; 1 Samuel 17:20; 1 Samuel 17:34-35; 1 Samuel 17:38-40; Psalms 23:1-6; Isaiah 40:11; Jeremiah 3:15; John 10:12.

items.question: In Ministerial Ethics, how should a pastor relate to another pastor's members?
items.text:
A pastor should treat another pastor's members with honour and restraint, never as his own to gather.

- **Do not use your exposure to draw away another pastor's people.** A travelling minister must not misuse the visibility an invitation gives him; to have a hidden agenda of starting a church nearby with some of your host pastor's members is like striking a friend below the belt, and Scripture warns that whoever repays good with evil will not escape trouble (Proverbs 17:13) [5]. For the same reason, a pastor should not invite a minister who wants to use his church as a launching pad or steal some of his members [4].

- **Show respect to the host's church and people.** When you are invited to speak, find something good to say about the host's church, the pastor and the choir, and never say things that make them look inferior [5].

- **Do not promote yourself among them.** Do not try to outshine the host pastor or make him look inferior, remembering that a prophet has no honour in his own country (John 4:44) [5].

- **Give honour to every minister present.** Show respect even to a pastor who visits your church but is not speaking, acknowledging his presence before the congregation [4].

- **Keep your own house in order.** Restrict the stream of visitors to your home, since members talk about what they saw there, and privacy shields you from critics and envious colleagues [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 8, 10 and 13 of *Ministerial Ethics*.

Scriptures referenced: Judges 3:20-21; 1 Chronicles 16:22; Proverbs 17:13; Matthew 10:8; John 4:44; Romans 13:7; Romans 15:24; Ephesians 4:16; Hebrews 7:7; 3 John 9.

items.question: How do I become a better leader of people?
items.text:
Becoming a better leader of people is a work of the heart and of wisdom, and our books have much to say about it.

- **See leadership as working on people, not holding a title.** To lead is to work on people until they become better human beings, the way Jesus transformed his disciples over three years, so that others marvelled that they had been with him [1].

- **Reproduce yourself in others so you are no longer essential.** A good leader prepares people for the day he will not be around, as Jesus did with his disciples, so that your absence will not matter because you have reproduced yourself in many others [3].

- **Ask God for wisdom, the master key to leading people.** By wisdom kings reign and lead their subjects forward; wisdom is the principal thing used to lead and to control human behaviour, which is no small task among difficult people [5].

- **Be at peace with those around you.** A leader does not bring more confusion but peace, following peace with all men (Hebrews 12:14); accept people as they are rather than trying to change everyone, and do not fight them over their successes [2].

- **Value every person.** Every person has a value, and people are attracted to places where they are valued; what you respect will come towards you, and every person who feels undervalued will move away [7].

- **Be real and go where you are asking others to go.** People do not want to follow a pretender; believe totally in where you are going, and lead by doing it yourself, for you cannot get people to pray if you do not pray yourself [8].

- **Become an encourager.** Notice when someone has made an effort, appreciate it even if you did not like it, say thank you for everything, and smile, for people gravitate around friendly people who accept them despite their failings [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 20, 23, 79, 86, 121 and 126 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 4 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*.

Scriptures referenced: Ruth 4:15; 1 Samuel 1:8; 2 Samuel 18:3; Proverbs 8:15-16; Proverbs 8:20; Matthew 10:17; Mark 1:17; John 16:4-5; John 16:16; John 16:23 and 5 more.

items.question: What should someone who just gave their life to Christ learn first?
items.text:
What a joy to hear of someone coming to Christ — that is the greatest treasure a person can receive [2].

The first thing to learn is that this is far more than joining a religion; it is the experience of a great change, a spiritual heart transplant, and understanding what has happened to you is what helps you grow in grace [7]. Then let them be taught the elementary principles of the faith, for how a person is grounded in those fundamentals permanently shapes their spiritual make-up [2]. They should also learn that following Jesus means sacrifice and daily following Him, not merely keeping rules [8]. And they should learn that ministry is possible alongside their other pursuits — they can be active in soul winning, prayer, and serving the Lord even while studying or working [3][4][6].

Finally, let them remember their Creator in the days of their youth, for it is important to come to God while young [8].

items.question: How can I spend time with God every morning without getting bored?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
What a good desire — to keep meeting God each morning and not let it go stale. Our books speak to this.

- **Feed your spirit on the Word, not just routine.** Your spirit grows by taking in the Word daily, so let Bible reading and study be the heart of the time, not a box to tick [1]. A daily dose of the Word increases your faith and keeps the time alive [7].

- **Come early and alone, like Moses.** Moses went up the mountain early in the morning to meet the Lord, carrying the tablets to write down what God would give him; you can have that same kind of quiet time, early and by yourself with God [1].

- **Draw near, and He draws near to you.** James 4:8 says that when you draw near to God, He draws near to you — so the time is not one-sided; it is fellowship, and fellowship is what keeps boredom away [2].

- **Let it refresh you.** The Word is like rain and snow that cools and refreshes the earth (Isaiah 55:10); a daily quiet time drives away weariness, dejection and depression, and you will feel its calming effect [7].

- **Vary how you take it in.** Besides reading, listen to preaching and watch services — faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17) [1].

- **Pray, and pray in the Spirit.** Talk to God, for you develop a relationship with anyone you talk to often [8], and praying in tongues builds you up in your faith [1][8].

- **Make it a habit, not a mood.** Good habits are difficult to form but easy to live with, and a daily quiet time is the most important habit of all [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell*, chapters 1, 3 and 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapter 9 of *Key Facts for New Believers*.

items.question: How can I encourage others who are going through hard times?
items.text:
What a kind question — wanting to strengthen others in their hard seasons is a good and holy desire.

- **Let your own troubles become your message.** Paul said he received a message from the Lord through the tribulations he experienced — a message of comfort for people in trouble — and the only way he could speak to those in trouble was to share what he had learned in his own [1]. As 2 Corinthians 1:4 says, God comforts us in every trouble so that we may be able to comfort those in any kind of trouble with the same comfort we received [1].

- **Remember how it felt, and reach out.** God warns us to remember our own hardships and to help others in a similar situation — if you came from poverty, you know what it feels like, and God expects you to reach out to the poor [5].

- **Show them examples of those who made it.** If you want to inspire pastors, show them ministers who have made it in ministry, and avoid dwelling on stories of those who fared badly, because that only brings discouragement and depression [6].

- **Share testimonies of what the Lord has done.** A testimony is an account of what the Lord did in someone else's life, and hearing them makes the simple wise — if He did it for them, He can do it for you [3].

- **Mourn with those who mourn.** Times of sorrow are among the most remembered times in people's lives; if you are by their side then, they will never forget you [8].

- **Give them encouraging messages to read.** There was great joy throughout the church when they read an encouraging message, and books can be the answer to a lonely or discouraged leader's problems [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *TS2. Hope Secrets*, chapter 22 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*, chapter 6 of *WOM13. The Big Secret - Your Ministry Depends on Books*, chapter 2 of *Those Who Forget* and chapters 11 and 20 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 30:6; Psalms 19:7; Proverbs 18:16; Acts 15:31; 2 Corinthians 1:3-5.

items.question: Different topic: how do I pray effectively?
items.text:
Prayer that works is not doodling and dawdling — it is prayer shaped by God's Word, offered with real passion, and given real time. Here are the ways the books set out.

- **Pray strategic Bible prayers.** Let your prayers be guided by the Word of God, praying the prayers recorded in Scripture — Ephesians 1:17-19 is one of the most powerful prayers a minister can pray, and Ephesians 3:15-19 prays to be grounded in love, which every pastor needs [1]. Become a Word person and believe the Word more than you believe in yourself [1].

- **Pray fervently.** Fervent prayer is ardent, passionate, zealous and eager — if someone watched you pray, they should be able to describe it with one of those words, and then you will have great results [1].

- **Pray in tongues.** Spend hours praying in the Spirit; Paul said, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [1]. When you pray in the Spirit, God directs your prayer Himself and gives you the words to say, and it builds you up like charging a battery (1 Corinthians 14:4) [7].

- **Have discussions with the Holy Spirit.** Prayer is a two-way affair — speak to the Holy Spirit and hear Him speak back, for He is our Comforter who teaches us all things (John 14:18, 26) [1].

- **Pray for a long time.** Jesus rose a great while before day and continued all night in prayer (Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12), and Paul prayed night and day exceedingly (1 Thessalonians 3:10) [1]. Start with one hour and graduate to three, then five and seven [7].

- **Pray repeatedly and habitually about God's will.** Jesus prayed the same words three times about the will of God — valuable repetition, not the vain repetitions Matthew 6:7 warns against [6]. For prayer to be effective it must be habitual, continuing in troubled times and in peace [2][8].

- **Use the right prayer for the moment.** There is the prayer of faith for the sick (James 5:15), the prayer confessing sins (1 John 1:8), and the short, powerful prayer — as when Jesus rebuked the storm and raised Lazarus — for crisis moments when there is no time to retreat [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*, chapters 1 and 7 of *How to Pray* and chapter 2 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 6:7; Mark 1:35; Mark 4:36-39; Mark 11:24; Luke 6:12; John 11:41-42; John 14:18; John 14:26; Acts 2:1-47; 1 Corinthians 13:3 and 10 more.

items.question: A young man in my fellowship told me he wants to kill himself. What should I do?
items.text:
I'm so glad he told you, and that you're carrying this with him — that is a heavy and holy moment.

Our books have not directly addressed this. They speak of the value of a person's life and of the anointing, and of the danger of destroying the opportunities God has set before someone [2][5], but they give no counsel on what to do when a person speaks of taking his own life.

Please don't carry this alone — bring it quickly to others who can help him in person, and stay close to him. If you'd like, we could look together at what the books say about the anointing and about cherishing what God has placed in a young life [2].

Please also speak with your shepherd or pastor today. Where a life may be at risk, contact emergency services or a medical professional now.
